title: Onboarding eval: bounded-sampling batching/cache/max_tokens sweep
content:
Purpose

Capture a compact, reproducible snapshot of a sweep we ran while onboarding model candidate `open-13b-instruct-v1` for hosted inference. The sweep explores the tradeoffs between tail latency and token-cost with three levers: batching, prefix/KV caching, and max_tokens (generation cap). This is a working note: rough charts in notebook, TODOs below.

Summary (high level observations)

- Small batches (1–4) + caching provide the best latency tail and maintain quality; for conversational prompt-set here caching yields 20–35% token cost reduction vs cache-off for same quality.
- Large batch sizes (>=8) reduce per-token cost substantially for long generations but increase p95 latency by 2–4x and induce more quality regressions on our instruction-following prompt set.
- Reducing max_tokens from 512->128 cuts cost and p95 dramatically for median-length prompts, with modest quality impact on the evaluation prompts used (pass-rate delta ~1.4% absolute). However, aggressive max_tokens (<=64) causes truncated completions and observed coherence drops.
- Best practical operating point for hosted inference (latency-focused SLOs, cost sensitivity moderate): batch=4, cache=on, max_tokens=256.

Context and constraints

- Model candidate: open-13b-instruct-v1 (mirrors family used in product onboarding).
- Prod-like runtime image: serving-runtime:main@2025-09-03 (CUDA kernels updated).
- Test infra: Dedicated small pool (4x A10g), single AZ, no multi-region.
- Prompt set: 120 examples, mixed conversational + instruction-following + code-synthesis; median reference target length ~140 tokens. See prompt_set_v3.csv in experiment artifacts.
- Budget: quick-turn evaluation for onboarding review (keep run time < 24h).
- Metrics tracked: latency p50/p95/p99, tokens-per-request (TPR), cost-per-request approximated by gpu_seconds*cost_rate, semantic-qa pass rate (binary correctness for instruction tasks), embedding-similarity-based quality (avg cosine to reference), and manual spot-check notes.

Experimental design

- Sweep axes:
  - batch_size: [1, 2, 4, 8, 16]
  - cache_mode: [off, prefix-kv-on]  (prefix-kv-on uses 5-min TTL, LRU eviction per-request)
  - max_tokens: [64, 128, 256, 512]
  - sampling: nucleus p=0.95 vs greedy (we keep sampling fixed to nuc=0.95 except a small control with greedy)
- For each config we ran the full 120 example prompt set twice to capture variance, randomizing order.
- Run concurrency was set to replicate production routing: 40 concurrent connections for batch>=4 tests, scaled down to 20 for batch=1 to avoid overwhelming scheduling.
- Logging: per-request trace with token counts, kernel selection, batch-formation latency, KV cache hits/misses, and model runtime fraction.

Key numbers (representative table; median of two runs)

Note: numbers rounded to 2 significant digits, units: ms for latency, tokens for TPR, cost units are normalized GPU-seconds per request.

1) batch=1, cache=off, max_tokens=256:
- p50: 120 ms, p95: 320 ms, p99: 520 ms
- TPR: 280 tokens
- cost_norm: 0.045
- semantic-qa pass: 86%
- observations: low variance, consistent quality.

2) batch=1, cache=on, max_tokens=256:
- p50: 110 ms, p95: 260 ms, p99: 420 ms
- TPR: 220 tokens (prefetch/prefix reuse saved ~21% tokens)
- cost_norm: 0.036 (≈20% cost saving)
- semantic-qa pass: 86%
- observations: cache hit rate ~32% across set; best improvement on chat prompts with shared system prompt.

3) batch=4, cache=on, max_tokens=256:
- p50: 150 ms, p95: 420 ms, p99: 860 ms
- TPR: 230 tokens
- cost_norm: 0.025 (best cost per request)
- semantic-qa pass: 84.5% (drop 1.5% vs batch=1)
- observations: large savings but p95 tail increased; batching introduces scheduling head-of-line for small latency SLOs.

4) batch=8, cache=on, max_tokens=256:
- p50: 190 ms, p95: 980 ms, p99: 1600 ms
- TPR: 260 tokens
- cost_norm: 0.02
- semantic-qa pass: 82% (regression noticeable in code-synthesis prompts where token interleaving caused temperature artifacts)

5) batch=4, cache=on, max_tokens=128:
- p50: 130 ms, p95: 360 ms, p99: 700 ms
- TPR: 150 tokens
- cost_norm: 0.0165
- semantic-qa pass: 84% (quality stable, few truncations)
- observations: sweet-spot for medium-length targets; reduces cost significantly.

6) batch=4, cache=on, max_tokens=64:
- p50: 90 ms, p95: 260 ms, p99: 480 ms
- TPR: 110 tokens
- cost_norm: 0.012
- semantic-qa pass: 80.6% (quality loss from truncation in ~9 prompts)

Control: greedy vs sampling (batch=1, max_tokens=256)
- greedy pass: 82% (more deterministic but lower pass on open-ended tasks)
- nuc0.95 pass: 86% (keeps diversity for creative prompts)

Interpretation and practical recommendation

- If strict p95 < 400 ms SLO, operate batch<=2 and cache ON; accept modest higher cost per token. Specifically: batch=2, cache=on, max_tokens=256 gives p95 ≈ 300 ms with pass ~85.5%.
- For cost-sensitive workloads where p95 can be relaxed to 500–700 ms, batch=4 + cache=on + max_tokens=128/256 gives the best unit economics.
- Avoid batch >=8 for instruction-following workloads where tail latency matters, unless you implement adaptive batching that collapses small-latency requests into a low-latency lane.

Failure modes observed (notes to self)

- Batching induced subtle quality regressions on multi-turn prompts where KV alignment interacts with batch-kernel optimizations. Hypothesis: scheduler groups prompts with different max_length distributions, causing kernel padding inefficiencies and temperature drift; need trace to confirm.
- Cache TTL=5m seemed okay for our set; but for high-variance user prompts cache hit rate will drop and prefix cache overhead might not justify cost.
- When concurrency > batch_size * 8 we observed queueing amplification on the host, leading to tail spikes. Scheduling knobs need to be tested with circuit-breakers.

Manual spot-checks (representative failures)

- Example ID 47: with batch=8 truncated code block mid-function at max_tokens=256, producing syntactically invalid code.
- Example ID 3: creative writing prompt with batch=4 produced repetition loop (temperature/kv interplay).

Open action items and experiments to run next

- Run an adaptive-batching experiment: low-latency lane (batch<=2) + batching lane (batch>=8) with request classifier based on prompt length. Measure overhead of lane routing.
- Re-run sweep with quantized model variant (4-bit) to measure cost delta and any extra quality regression. Add regression harness to detect grammatical errors.
- Instrument kernel-level padding inefficiency metrics to validate scheduling hypothesis. Add a per-batch pad_ratio metric to logs.
- Evaluate cache TTL sensitivity: test TTLs [30s, 2m, 5m, 15m] and plot net cost vs hit-rate tradeoff.
- Add an automated truncation detector to evaluation harness that flags cut-off completions (identify tokens with abrupt ending and invalid punctuation).

Repro commands and artifacts

- Notebook: experiments/onboard/sweep_snapshot_v2025-09-12.ipynb (attached to PR, see linked_artifacts)
- Run script: infra/experiments/run_sweep.sh --model open-13b-instruct-v1 --batch-sizes 1,2,4,8,16 --cache-modes off,on --max-tokens 64,128,256,512 --repeats 2
- Log archive: gs://redwood-internal-qa/onboard/eval-snapshot-2025-09-12.tar.gz
- Quick grep for failure traces: 
  grep -E "TRUNCATION|KV_MISS|PAD_RATIO>" logs/*.json | head -n 200

Notes for onboarding review

- Bring these single-pool numbers to the candidate model review: highlights are strong per-token cost when batching, but tail latency is the gating factor for our hosted SLOs. Recommend allowing batch=4 for Dedicated contracts but restrict to batch<=2 in Hosted tier with automatic adaptive fallback to reasonable batch lanes.
- We should add a one-pager summarizing the recommended default runtime profile for new 13B-class models (batch cap, cache default, max_tokens default). Draft below and merge into product onboarding checklist.

Draft one-pager blurb (for checklist)

- Default runtime profile (13B class, latency-first): batch_cap=2, cache=on, max_tokens=256, sampling=nucleus(0.95).
- Cost-first profile (Dedicated/enterprise): batch_cap=8, cache=on, max_tokens=128 (with warning about possible truncation).
- Add automated quality regression alarms for semantic-qa pass rate drop >2% vs baseline.

Misc scratch/thoughts

- Could we get a fast-path for short prompts (<60 tokens) that bypasses batching? Might avoid majority of p95 spikes.
- Look into per-request kernel hints (force small-kernel for short-sequence prompts) to reduce pad inflation.

TODO (immediate)

- [ ] Run TTL sensitivity sweep.
- [ ] Add pad_ratio to tracing.
- [ ] Draft one-pager and attach to onboarding PR.
- [ ] Schedule 30m sync with Console team to discuss SLOs and lane routing.
